analysis.one_liner: Replaces patent monopolies on HIV/AIDS drugs with government prize payments, opening the drugs to generic competition.
analysis.headline: The bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it died in the Senate Health Committee with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strip patents and other exclusive marketing rights from every drug, vaccine, or biologic certified as an HIV/AIDS treatment, effective October 1, 2014. Instead of recouping research costs through high monopoly prices, drug developers would be paid cash prizes from a government fund, judged on how many patients benefit and how much the treatment improves on existing options. At least 5% of prizes would reward open sharing of research, and a separate fund would reward companies that let low-cost generics reach developing countries. The fund would be paid for by a fee on large health insurers and an annual appropriation of about 0.02% of GDP.
analysis.who_benefits: The roughly 1.1 million Americans living with HIV, who would pay generic prices for their antiretroviral drugs instead of brand-name prices — in a field where public and private spending on these drugs already exceeds $9 billion a year. Insurers, employers, and federal programs like Medicaid and Medicare would also pay less. Drug developers would still be rewarded, but through prizes rather than the right to charge monopoly prices.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People living with HIV and their insurers

how_it_helps.text: The bill would deny any person exclusive rights to manufacture, distribute, or sell a certified HIV/AIDS treatment or its manufacturing process, including patent rights, pediatric extensions, orphan drug exclusivity, and the 30-month delay that brand-name makers can impose on generic competitors.

In place of those monopoly rights, innovators would receive prize payments from a Prize Fund for HIV/AIDS, with amounts set by criteria including the number of patients who benefit and the treatment's incremental benefit over existing drugs, capped at 50% of the fund per treatment and 10 fiscal years of payments.

At least 5% of prize payments would be dedicated to Open Source Dividend Prizes, rewarding people and communities that shared knowledge, data, and technology royalty-free, with a public nomination process.

A separate Donor Innovation Prize Fund would reward owners who unpatent or openly license HIV treatments in developing countries, funded in part by setting aside 10% of the estimated federal cost of treatments used by PEPFAR, to bring down generic prices abroad.
The fund would be financed by an annual appropriation equal to 0.02% of GDP plus a fee on health insurers with more than $25 million in premiums, allocated by net premiums written.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug makers would lose the patent monopoly revenue on HIV/AIDS treatments, which are currently a multi-billion-dollar-a-year market. Large health insurers would pay a new annual fee. Taxpayers would cover the federal appropriation of roughly 0.02% of GDP each year — several billion dollars — even as spending on the drugs themselves falls.
analysis.who_pays_short: Brand-name drug makers and large health insurers

drawbacks.text: The prize system would replace the patent system for a whole disease category with an untested mechanism; how well it works would depend heavily on how the Prize Fund Director sets award criteria, and developers who judge future prizes unreliable might simply avoid HIV research.

The prize fund is only about 0.02% of GDP per year while current spending on HIV antiretrovirals already exceeds $9 billion annually, so if prize payments plus the new mechanism proved insufficient to attract investment, research would slow without an easy way to turn the policy off.
The new fee would fall on health insurers, who could pass part of it to premiums, and the mandatory appropriation would compete with other federal spending priorities.

The bill covers only HIV/AIDS, which would treat one disease's innovation incentives differently from every other disease's and could complicate development of combination products that treat HIV and other conditions together.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For people with HIV, insurers, and federal programs, the savings could be large: cutting monopoly pricing on a $9-billion-a-year drug market in exchange for a smaller fund makes the arithmetic favorable for buyers. The real uncertainty is on the innovation side — prize systems of this scale have not been used before, and the bill's success would depend entirely on how a fund director sized and timed awards. It is an ambitious, honestly designed experiment with real execution risk, not a hidden giveaway; the bill even includes caps, transparency rules, and an arbitration process for splitting prizes among patent owners.

outcome.mechanism: Sanders introduced the bill in March 2013 and it was referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it sat until the 113th Congress ended in January 2015 — no hearing, no markup, no vote, and no cosponsor ever signed on.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the Prize Fund for HIV/AIDS Act on March 20, 2013, to replace patent exclusivity on HIV/AIDS treatments with prize payments.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions the same day; that referral is the last recorded action.
No other senator cosponsored the bill.
The committee never held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it died when the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug makers kept their patent monopolies and monopoly prices on HIV/AIDS treatments, and the health insurers who would have paid the new fund fee avoided it. No one who advocated for lower HIV drug prices came out ahead.

for.name: Sen. Bernard Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 20, 2013; it was his only recorded action on it in the chamber.

against.name: Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions (chaired by Sen. Tom Harkin)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day of introduction and took no further action; no hearing, markup, or vote was ever recorded.

against.name: Pharmaceutical industry
against.role: Holder of the patent exclusivities the bill would repeal
against.what_they_did: No industry opposition campaign is documented in the provided sources; the bill never advanced far enough to force a recorded fight.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no cosponsor joined, so there is no record of where members stood beyond the single independent sponsor; the bill never got far enough to reveal a partisan split.

industries.note: They would lose all patents and exclusive marketing rights on HIV/AIDS treatments and the manufacturing processes behind them, ending the ability to charge monopoly prices for drugs whose U.S. spending already tops $9 billion a year. They would be compensated through prizes, but prize amounts would be set by a government director rather than the market. Their gain under the status quo comes directly from what patients, insurers, and the federal government pay for the drugs.

Insurers with more than $25 million in premiums would pay an annual fee to finance the prize fund, allocated by their share of net premiums. They would also save substantially on antiretroviral costs as those drugs moved to generic competition, so the net effect on them is mixed.

With exclusivity eliminated, any manufacturer could make certified HIV/AIDS treatments, and the Donor Innovation Prize Fund would further open developing-country markets through the Medicine Patent Pool. Their gain is the public's lower prices.

industries.industry: Open-source and nonprofit medical research community
industries.note: At least 5% of prize payments would be reserved for Open Source Dividend Prizes, and nonprofit intermediaries could compete to manage interim research rewards — new funding streams for researchers who share data and technology freely.
